The Story

## Fifteen years building the same idea, better each time

He spent a decade building Opex Analytics from a blank whiteboard to 140 employees. Then he helped orchestrate a $1.5 billion exit. Then he started over.

Ganesh Ramakrishna trained as a mechanical engineer in Mumbai, then crossed an ocean to earn a master's degree in operations research at Purdue University. That combination — physical systems thinking married to mathematical optimization — became the throughline of everything that followed.

Before founding anything, he ran global leadership roles at IBM. Long enough to see how enterprises actually use software. Long enough to develop strong opinions about how they shouldn't.

In 2010, he co-founded Opex Analytics in Chicago. The premise was simple and the execution was not: build custom AI and machine learning solutions for Fortune 500 companies trying to make better decisions about their supply chains. Over nine years, Opex grew to 140 people. The work was real. The clients were household names. And in October 2019, LLamasoft acquired Opex to form what it called an "applied AI" powerhouse in supply chain analytics.

Ganesh stayed. As Senior Vice President, he ran the combined business and — in a move that most founders never get to witness — watched the company he helped build become part of a $1.5 billion acquisition when Coupa Software bought LLamasoft in 2020.

Most people would have stopped there. Ganesh started taking notes.

> "When we started Lyric, our mission was simple — recognizing that no two supply chains are alike, which is why Lyric was built to be composable from the start, allowing teams to configure solutions that align with their specific needs rather than bending their business to fit rigid software."

— Ganesh Ramakrishna, Lyric Founder & CEO

In 2021, Ganesh founded Lyric with a specific thesis: the supply chain software industry had built the wrong thing for thirty years. Every major platform asked companies to conform to its data model, its workflow logic, its definition of what a supply chain problem looks like. The result was expensive implementations, low adoption, and decisions made on stale data by analysts who couldn't wait for IT.

Lyric took the opposite position. The platform is composable — meaning teams can assemble the decision models they need from modular building blocks, rather than inheriting whatever the vendor decided. It's AI-native, meaning optimization, simulation, and forecasting are structural features, not bolt-ons. And it's fast to deploy: where legacy platforms take quarters to implement, Lyric measures onboarding in weeks.

The results arrived quickly. Lyric emerged from stealth and within 18 months had achieved 500% revenue growth. By mid-2025, nearly 30 global enterprises had signed on — names like Coca-Cola, Mondelez International, Owens & Minor, Estée Lauder, and Google. A Coca-Cola supply chain executive put it bluntly: "The marriage of managing your data and actually using it in modeling — all in one place — that was the difference maker."

In August 2025, Lyric closed a $43.5M Series B led by Insight Partners, bringing total funding to $67 million. The round included Primary Venture Partners, Permanent Capital Ventures, VMG Partners, PSP Growth, and NewBuild Venture Capital — a coalition that stretches from enterprise software specialists to consumer growth investors betting on AI infrastructure.

What Lyric Does

## Not a supply chain tool. A supply chain operating system.

Lyric is what you get when you take everything wrong with legacy supply chain software and rebuild it from scratch with AI as the core, not the feature.

Composable

Build what you need

Modular architecture means teams configure decision models specific to their supply chain — not the vendor's template. No two supply chains are alike. Lyric assumes that from the start.

AI-Native

Optimization at the core

Simulation, forecasting, and machine learning are structural. Lyric integrates NVIDIA cuOpt for GPU-accelerated route and network optimization. Agentic AI handles disruption response in real time.

Fast Deploy

Weeks, not quarters

Where legacy platforms require months of custom implementation, Lyric's reusable supply chain logic library and no-code workflow tools put decision intelligence in the hands of teams fast.

Ganesh didn't pivot every two years. He spent a decade at Opex building deep domain credibility before his first exit. Then spent another four years building the harder thing.

### On inventory and the math behind good decisions

In a technical interview, Ganesh explained the compounding problem of rule-of-thumb supply chain policies: "If you work hard to reduce lead times and have a rule-of-thumb policy, there is no automatic way to reduce inventory. With a good formula in place, the formula's output will give you less inventory as the lead time decreases."

That's the Ganesh Ramakrishna thesis in one sentence: when you have the right model, improvements cascade automatically. When you don't, every efficiency gain requires manual re-calibration. The entire Lyric platform exists to give enterprises the right model.

He's been making this argument — in different forms — since before Opex Analytics existed. After two companies and a $1.5 billion exit, the argument is backed by something more than theory.

Raising VC Money and Building Lyric


On the Decision Intelligence Lab podcast, Ganesh was unusually frank about the things that don't get discussed in founder mythology: the moments when fundraising fails, the discipline required to not pivot on every market signal, and what "product-market fit" actually means when your customer is a Fortune 500 supply chain team that moves at a very different pace than a software company.

What's Next

## The Series B is fuel, not finish line

With $43.5M in new capital, Lyric's roadmap is specific: accelerate the product, expand the library of reusable supply chain logic, deepen AI-driven capabilities for experimentation, simulation, and automation. And invest heavily in customer success — because in enterprise software, the sale is just the beginning.

Ganesh has also been explicit about where the industry is heading: agentic AI for supply chain. Not AI that surfaces insights for a human to act on — AI that closes the loop autonomously. Lyric's platform is designed to get there. The digital twin capabilities, the simulation models, the synthetic data generation — all of it is infrastructure for supply chains that don't just report on disruptions but respond to them.

The aspiration is large: to build the foundational AI infrastructure layer for global supply chain decision-making. A composable, adaptive platform so reliable that it becomes the operating system on which enterprises run their supply chain thinking.

> "We are proud to be building the next generation of supply chain infrastructure."

— Ganesh Ramakrishna, on closing Lyric's Series B
